Also called the minor blues or hexatonic blues scale. On C, in its standard textbook form: C E♭ F G♭ G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 1 1 3 2. Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor with an added ♭5.

The blues came out of African American vocal music in the Deep South around . Its "blue notes" are inflected regions around the third, fifth and seventh that a singer or guitarist bends into, and they fall between equal-tempered pitches.
's published blues, among them "The Memphis Blues" ( ) and "St. Louis Blues" ( ), had to fit those inflections onto a piano. Notation and keyboards turned the blue notes into fixed lowered pitches.
The six-note blues scale is a later pedagogical summary of that practice, popularized by mid- jazz method books.
Blues harmony is a sequence of dominant seventh chords (I7, IV7, V7). The melody's ♭3 against the chord's major third is the idiom's central dissonance, and players often slide from ♭3 to 3.
Rock guitar improvisation is built largely on minor pentatonic and blues-scale patterns.
A "major blues" scale adds ♭3 to Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major: C D E♭ E G A on C.
The chromatic run F G♭ G gives players a fixed-pitch stand-in for a bend through the blue fifth.

The MicroFreak manual lists its "Blues" setting as nine notes: C D E♭ F G♭ G A♭ A B♭. That collection is the hexatonic blues scale plus 2, ♭6 and 6, larger than any standard blues scale. The same manual's introduction to scales says blues scales use six notes. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings and Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales.
The Launchpad manual names a "Blues" setting without listing its pitches.
Also called the protus authentic mode or Mode 1. On C: C D E♭ F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 2 1 2. The second mode of Music/Scale/Major.

The name is Greek but the scale is not. The ancient Greek Dorian octave species ran from E to E in modern terms, the collection now called Phrygian. Carolingian theorists, most visibly the anonymous Alia musica around , attached the Greek names to the church modes in a different order.
In plainchant and Renaissance polyphony, the D mode was defined by its final, its range and its reciting tone A. B♭ was common, so much Dorian music sounds Aeolian to modern ears.

Baroque composers often wrote D minor with no key signature, a habit inherited from Dorian notation. 's Toccata and Fugue in D minor BWV 538 is called "Dorian" for that reason alone: its notation has no flat, and its music is in D minor.
Modal jazz made Dorian a vamp scale. 's "So What" (Kind of Blue, ) sits on D Dorian with a bridge in E♭ Dorian, and 's "Impressions" uses the same form.
The i–IV vamp, a minor tonic with a major subdominant, is Dorian's signature in rock and Latin music, as in 's "Oye Como Va" and the rock band Santana's cover of it, with on guitar.
English and Celtic folk melodies, among them "Scarborough Fair", are often Dorian.
In jazz chord-scale theory it is the default scale for a minor seventh chord functioning as ii.
Its step pattern is a palindrome, so Dorian is the only diatonic mode that inverts to itself about its tonic. D is the center of symmetry of the white-key collection.
The raised sixth makes IV a major triad and puts a tritone between ♭3 and 6. That raised sixth is the note a listener uses to tell Dorian from Aeolian.
Music/Scale/Dorian/Ukrainian and Music/Scale/Dorian/Bebop carry Dorian in their names. Ukrainian Dorian derives from harmonic minor, and Bebop Dorian adds a chromatic passing tone.
The MicroFreak manual spells its "Dorian" and "Minor" settings almost identically; the "Minor" spelling is this scale with an added B natural. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings.
Also called the bebop minor scale. On C, in the form most reference lists give: C D E♭ E F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 1 1 2 2 1 2. Music/Scale/Dorian with an added chromatic passing tone.
The bebop scales are a teaching abstraction of the eighth-note lines of , and their contemporaries. 's method books from the popularized the family: bebop dominant, bebop major and bebop minor.
The names came decades after the music. They describe a habit of chromatic passing tones that pedagogy later fixed into eight-note collections.
An eight-note scale run in eighth notes from a chord tone on the beat puts chord tones on every downbeat.

With the added major third, the collection equals the bebop dominant scale a fourth above (F G A B♭ C D E♭ E). A line descending from F puts F, E♭, C and A on the beats, so one line serves both chords of a ii–V in B♭, Cm7 and F7.
With the added major seventh, a line descending from C puts C, B♭, G and E♭ on the beats, the chord tones of Cm7 itself.
The added note is a passing tone, never a resting point.
Sources disagree on which note to add. The major-seventh form, C D E♭ F G A B♭ B, matches the MicroFreak manual's spelling of its "Minor" setting in Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings.
The Launchpad manual names a "Bebop Dorian" setting without listing its pitches.
Also called Romanian minor, Dorian ♯4 and, in klezmer, Mi sheberakh or Av harachamim. On C: C D E♭ F♯ G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 3 1 2 1 2. The fourth mode of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic.

The scale belongs to the folk and liturgical music of Ukraine, Romania and Moldova and the Ashkenazi Jewish communities that lived among them. Klezmer musicians named it after the Sabbath prayer Mi sheberakh, whose cantorial setting uses it.
The Western names are descriptive labels from scale catalogues. Practitioners name it by its prayer or by the genre that uses it.
Klezmer doinas, the free-rhythm improvisations that open a suite, often sit in this mode, as do many Romanian and Ukrainian dance tunes.
The augmented second ♭3–♯4 is the mode's signature figure. Melodies circle around ♯4 and resolve it up to 5 or down to ♭3.

The name says Dorian, and the only change from Music/Scale/Dorian is the raised fourth. Its pitches still come from harmonic minor a fifth below: C Ukrainian Dorian uses the notes of G harmonic minor.
Over a tonic minor triad, the ♯4 and 6 together outline a diminished-seventh sonority (F♯ A C E♭), which gives a static tonic a strong pull toward the dominant.
From hirajōshi, "even tuning", a standard tuning of the Japanese koto. On C, in the form most Western references give: C D E♭ G A♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 4 1 4.
Hirajōshi is a tuning for the thirteen strings of the koto, credited to in the . It became the standard tuning for solo koto music of the Edo period, including his Rokudan no shirabe.
Western scale catalogues and guitar method books lifted the tuning's pitches out as a five-note scale in the . Japanese theory treats the same pitches as the miyako-bushi or in scale.
In Western rock, metal and film music, the scale stands in for Japan.
Western references disagree about which note is the tonic: 0 2 3 7 8 and 0 4 6 7 11 both appear in print. They are rotations of one pitch set, the same set as the miyako-bushi scale 0 1 5 7 8.

It is a hemitonic pentatonic, the opposite of : two of its five steps are semitones, each followed by a major third. That pairing gives it a sound unlike the semitone-free Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.
The Launchpad manual names a "Hirajoshi" setting without listing its pitches.
Also called Ionian and natural major. On C: C D E F G A B. Steps in semitones: 2 2 1 2 2 2 1.

Medieval theory recognized eight modes on the finals D, E, F and G, defined by final, range and reciting tone. A mode on C circulated in practice, often as a Lydian with B♭, but had no name in the system.
's Dodecachordon ( ) expanded the system to twelve modes and named the C mode Ionian, alongside Aeolian on A. Zarlino later renumbered the modes to start on C, which put Ionian first.

Over the Ionian and Aeolian absorbed the other modes into major-minor tonality. 's Traité de l'harmonie ( ) grounded the major triad in the resonance of a vibrating body and gave major its theoretical priority.
The solmization syllables ut re mi fa sol la come from 's hexachord, taken from the hymn Ut queant laxis in the . The seventh syllable, si (later ti), was added much later.
The reference collection for common-practice tonality, Western pedagogy and most popular music. Every other diatonic mode is described as an alteration of it.
Its association with brightness or happiness is learned. The MicroFreak manual's chapter on scales says as much in Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales.

The diatonic collection is a stack of six perfect fifths (F C G D A E B). Its interval-class vector is 254361: each interval class appears a different number of times. Because the tritone appears once, a listener who hears F–B can locate the tonic; resolving that tritone inward to E–C is the core of the dominant-seventh resolution.

In five-limit just intonation the scale needs two sizes of whole tone, 9:8 and 10:9. D–A then comes out a syntonic comma narrow of a pure fifth, so the ii triad is out of tune in a just C major. This is the textbook case for temperament.
Inverting the step pattern about the tonic produces Music/Scale/Phrygian. Inverting Mixolydian produces Music/Scale/Minor/Natural, and Music/Scale/Dorian inverts to itself.
The pitch-class complement of the major scale is Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major: on a piano, white keys against black keys.
Spelled Marva on the Launchpad. In sargam: S r G M' P D N. On C: C D♭ E F♯ G A B. Steps in semitones: 1 3 2 1 2 2 1.
classified Hindustani ragas under ten parent scales, or thaats, in the early , and named each after a prominent raga. Marwa is one of the ten.
A thaat is a classification. Ragas live inside it, each with its own phrases, ascent and descent, emphasized notes and performance time; a thaat itself is never performed.
The Carnatic system's equivalent parent scale is Gamanashrama, melakarta 53.
Raga Marwa, a sunset raga, omits Pa entirely and centers on komal Re and Dha.
Ragas Puriya and Sohini use the same notes with different emphasis: Puriya dwells in the lower register around Ni and Ga, and Sohini in the upper register around high Sa.
The thaat has both a raised fourth and a lowered second, so the tonic is approached by a half step from either side (N–S and r–S).

Hindustani pitches are tuned by ear against the tanpura drone and do not match equal temperament. The equal-tempered spelling on a Launchpad approximates the collection without its intonation or melodic rules.
On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Natural with a raised seventh.
The raised seventh came from cadential practice: musica ficta supplied a leading tone at cadences in modal polyphony long before any theorist listed the result as a scale.
"Harmonic minor" is a pedagogical name. It collects the pitches of the chords of a minor key, with the dominant and leading-tone chords built on the raised seventh.
Common-practice harmony uses the collection for V, V7 and vii°7 in minor. Its melodies avoid the augmented second between ♭6 and 7, or fill it in, or turn it into a deliberate effect.
exoticism made that augmented second a marker of the East, Spain or Romani music.
Its fifth mode, C D♭ E F G A♭ B♭ on C, is Phrygian dominant. Flamenco, klezmer (where it is called Freygish or Ahava Rabbah) and Middle Eastern pop use it, and the maqam Hijaz is close to it.
The collection contains a fully diminished seventh chord (B D F A♭) and an augmented triad (E♭ G B). Those two symmetrical chords give it more harmonic ambiguity than the diatonic modes.

The MicroFreak manual lists its "Harmonic Minor" setting as C D E F G A♭ B. With E natural, that collection is harmonic major, 's name for a major scale with a lowered sixth. The manual page is Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings; which collection the firmware plays is not documented there.
Also called Gypsy minor and double harmonic minor. On C: C D E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 3 1 1 3 1. Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic with a raised fourth.

The name comes from the style hongrois: the verbunkos idiom that Romani bands played in Hungarian cities, which , and borrowed. Liszt's book on the subject, Des Bohémiens et de leur musique en Hongrie ( ), credited that music to the Roma.

and 's fieldwork after found that older Hungarian peasant song was largely pentatonic. The "Hungarian" in the scale's name therefore names an urban, Romani-performed popular style rather than Hungarian village song. See Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies and the "alla zingarese" finales of Brahms and draw on the idiom, usually as melodic color over functional harmony in harmonic minor.
Its two augmented seconds, ♭3–♯4 and ♭6–7, make it a quick shorthand for Eastern Europe in film and game scores.
It has two leading tones: F♯ leads to G and B leads to C. A melody can cadence on the dominant as strongly as on the tonic.
The step pattern 2 1 3 1 1 3 1 read backward is a rotation of itself, so the collection maps onto itself under inversion.
It is the fourth mode of the double harmonic major scale (C D♭ E F G A♭ B), which Arabic theory associates with maqam Hijaz Kar.

Also called jazz minor and, in its ascending form, the acoustic collection. On C, ascending: C D E♭ F G A B. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 2 2 1. The classical descending form is Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.

The classical form records voice leading. Raising both sixth and seventh on the way up avoids the augmented second of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic while keeping the leading tone. Lowering both on the way down lets the line fall toward the dominant.
Baroque lines follow the harmony more than the direction. Over a dominant chord, 's descending lines keep the raised sixth and seventh.

jazz theory uses the ascending form in both directions and treats each of its modes as a chord-scale. 's Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization ( ) brought Lydian-based thinking into that theory.
Its modes cover much of jazz harmony beyond the diatonic system:
Mode 1, melodic minor on its own tonic, fits a minor-major seventh chord.
